title: When Someone Benefits From the Problem
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article examines the common organizational puzzle of a well-diagnosed problem with an agreed-upon solution that somehow never gets fixed. Using an example of a company running dozens of redundant internal communication channels, it argues that unaddressed problems usually persist because someone influential quietly benefits from the status quo, whether through control, cover, or avoided embarrassment. The piece suggests that naming this dynamic, rather than being baffled by organizational inertia, is more useful for those who genuinely want change. It ends with a pragmatic recommendation: rather than fight self-interested resistance, redirect energy toward problems others are actually willing to solve.
points: Diagnoses persistent unsolved problems as evidence someone benefits from inaction
Uses a real-world example of an organization with 86 redundant communication channels
Explains how ambiguity or lack of clarity can serve a powerful stakeholder's interests
Recommends disengaging from self-interested blockers rather than fighting them
quotes: One of the many head-scratchers in organizational life is when a known problem never gets addressed.
Any time a well-dissected problem and an elegant solution remain untouched by an organization, team, or leader, there is one known cause.
Because the organization has too many outlets, team members don’t know where to turn to learn the most essential messages.
Someone on the leadership team benefits from having 86 mediums.
But the fact remains that someone influential benefits from not solving the problem.
In too many organizations, powerful leaders too often engage in self-interested behavior to the detriment of the organization.
